name: Feeding America: food network (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Feeding America's food network and SNAP help in the US.
summary: Feeding America sources donated food from about 600 national food companies for the US network of more than 250 food banks and 60,000 pantries, funds and supports those food banks, and helps people apply for SNAP. In the year to June 2025 it spent $222 million of its own money on this and passed on 2.4 billion pounds of donated food (about 2 billion meals), which, valued at what it saves the households who eat it on the site's log-income scale and credited by Feeding America's small share of the resources behind it (the donors' food at about $5.7 billion at retail and the food banks' and pantries' cost of handing it out), with the SNAP enrolments its grants help cause and the landfill emissions the donated food avoids, comes to about 0.017 years of healthy life per $1,000. It is low because the people helped are in the US, where $90 of food a year is a small share of what even a poor household spends, and because most of the resources behind the food are others'. About three fifths is the food, the rest SNAP help; both branches are discounted for missing data. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the food would have reached people without Feeding America, how poor the people served are, and how many SNAP enrolments the help causes.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Spending on the food network programmes, FY2025 (year to 30 June 2025), net of what members paid back
rows.explainer: Member services, food procurement and programs, the three lines that get food and food help to people, in Feeding America's own cash (the audited statement of functional expenses before donated goods), less the food procurement revenue the member food banks paid back for food and transport bought for them: their own money passing through Feeding America's books. Fiscal year 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025, the latest with both audited accounts and the annual report's reach. The donated food itself ($4.58 billion at wholesale) is the food donors' resource and enters the credit share below, not this cost. Policy and advocacy, research and analysis and public awareness have their own model (feeding-america-charityevals-advocacy).

rows.explainer: All of Feeding America's cash expenses (programmes, management, fundraising), before the donated food, media and services it books at fair value, less the members' repayments for food bought on their behalf.

rows.label: Programme expenses in cash, net of members' repayments, FY2025
rows.explainer: All six programme lines in cash, less the members' repayments: the base over which management and fundraising ($82 million) are spread.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)

rows.explainer: Pantry food is chosen by others: some items go unused or replace cheaper ones. Most of it frees money the household would spend on food anyway (about $90 a person a year against food budgets of thousands), so it is close to cash. 0.8, the same judgment as the Salvation Army build's food and goods (0.6 to 1), range 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: The shared figure for people getting US food aid, pantry food or SNAP (@united_states.food_aid_recipients_consumption_share, 30%, range 20-50%): pantry clients are mostly at or below the poverty line, poorer than the poorest fifth of households on average. The Salvation Army build reads the same figure.

Years the help keeps its money value for the people served

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the clients' own consumption: a dollar does far less for a US household than for one living on a few dollars a day.

rows.explainer: 0: no deaths are counted (above); kept so the shared value of a death stays in the model.

rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: SNAP: share of the applications helped that are approved
rows.explainer: No published approval rate for the network's assisted applications; the help is aimed at people screened as likely eligible, but many applications fail on paperwork or interviews. 0.6, range 0.4 to 0.8.

source.title: Congressional Research Service, SNAP: A Primer on Eligibility and Benefits (R42505, 4 November 2026)
source.quote: In FY2025, an average of 42.4 million individuals in 22.6 million households participated in SNAP each month.

rows.explainer: The same sentence: households, to turn applications (one per household) into people.

rows.label: SNAP: people per participating household
SNAP: average monthly benefit per household, FY2025 (US$)

source.title: Congressional Research Service, SNAP: A Primer on Eligibility and Benefits (R42505, 4 November 2026)
source.quote: Monthly benefits averaged $188.30 per person and $353.43 per household.

rows.explainer: The national average benefit per household; the households the help enrols get less (snap_marginal_benefit_ratio).

rows.label: SNAP: benefit per person per year (US$)
SNAP: benefit of the households the help enrols, against the average benefit
rows.explainer: Households enrolled by outreach are less needy than those who enrol unaided and get smaller benefits on average (Finkelstein and Notowidigdo 2019 find the marginal enrollees in their trial less poor and with lower benefits than existing participants). 0.8, range 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: SNAP: what a dollar of benefits is worth against a dollar of cash
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@snap.cash_equivalence, 0.95): most SNAP households spend more on food than their benefit, so it frees cash. The advocacy model reads the same figure.

rows.label: SNAP: share of the programme's cost paid out as benefits
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@snap.benefit_share, 0.92): taxpayers pay the administration too, so the payers' cost is the benefit over this. The advocacy model reads the same figure.

rows.label: SNAP: years a household helped to enrol stays on the programme
rows.explainer: New entrants' spells are short: USDA's studies of SNAP participation dynamics find many spells end within a year, and many who leave come back later. 1.5 years, range 9 months to 3 years. Recertification needs no further help from the food bank.

rows.label: SNAP: people enrolled through the applications helped
SNAP: ln(consumption) gain per person enrolled, discounted
rows.formula: snap_cash_equivalence * ln(1 + snap_benefit_per_person_year * snap_marginal_benefit_ratio / baseline_consumption) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, snap_years)
rows.explainer: The benefit of the households the help enrols, at the shared value of SNAP against cash, at the same clients' consumption as the food branch, over the years on the programme, discounted.

rows.label: Marginal cost of public funds: what a dollar of public money costs those who pay, in dollars
rows.explainer: The shared marginal cost of public funds (@public_funds.mcpf, 1.2, range 1 to 1.5, anchored on Dahlby 2008): what a dollar of SNAP costs the taxpayers who pay for it, as every model that counts the cost of public money reads it.

rows.label: How the federal taxes behind SNAP fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: The shared figure for how US federal taxes fall (@public_funds.us_federal_payer_multiple, 1.4, range 1 to 2): SNAP is paid for by the federal income tax and borrowing, which fall mostly on richer households.

rows.label: SNAP: ln(consumption) given up by those who pay, per person enrolled
rows.formula: snap_benefit_per_person_year * snap_marginal_benefit_ratio / snap_benefit_share * mcpf / (payer_multiple * @united_states.ce_expenditure_per_person_2024) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, snap_years)
rows.explainer: The benefit and its administration are a transfer from taxpayers: what they cost them on the same log scale, at the household survey's consumption per person (the recipients' scale, docs/normalization.md 2.14), times the cost of raising public money, as the advocacy model and the Habitat for Humanity advocacy build count government money.

rows.label: SNAP: net ln(consumption) gain per person enrolled
Food: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The pounds and their value are audited and the value of food to a household is its price; the doubts are about the food mix (some items low in value to the household, such as beverages and snacks) beyond the in-kind discount above. 0.95, range 0.8 to 1, near the Salvation Army build's food and goods (0.9 to 1).

rows.label: Food: share that wouldn't have reached people without Feeding America
rows.explainer: Without Feeding America's national contracts and retail pickup programme, some donors would give straight to local food banks or other networks and some food would go to salvage, animal feed or landfill; and people helped would partly turn to other pantries or family. 0.5, range 0.25 to 0.8, as the Salvation Army build's food and goods (0.3 to 0.8).

rows.label: Food banks' and pantries' cost to store and hand out a pound, including volunteers' time (US$)
rows.explainer: Member food banks and their 60,000 partner pantries and meal programmes collect, sort, store and hand out the food, with paid staff, trucks, warehouses and volunteers (most pantries are run by volunteers, valued at the US volunteer hour, @united_states.volunteer_hour_value_2025, $36). The shared maintenance fee food banks may charge pantries is about 20 cents a pound and covers only part of the food banks' cost; with the pantries' volunteer hours, 25 cents in all, range 10 to 80 cents.

rows.label: Share of Feeding America's cost behind its SNAP work
rows.explainer: The programs line ($37 million, a sixth of the modelled cost) pays for SNAP outreach, child hunger and food-as-medicine grants; about a third of it for SNAP help is about 6% of the whole cost, range 3% to 12%.

rows.label: SNAP: cost of the network's help per application (all funders, US$)
rows.explainer: Screening, help with the forms and documents, and follow-up through the interview: a few hours of trained staff or volunteer time per application, with outreach to find the applicants. $150, range $75 to $300. Food banks' outreach is paid for largely by state SNAP outreach contracts (half federally reimbursed) and their own funds; Feeding America's grants are the rest.

rows.label: Food: Feeding America's share of the resources behind the food reaching people
rows.formula: cost_total * (1 - snap_program_share) / (cost_total * (1 - snap_program_share) + @feeding_america.donated_food_value_fy2025 * retail_vs_wholesale + fa_pounds * distribution_cost_per_lb)
rows.explainer: Convention 2: Feeding America's own cash against the donors' food at its retail value (the audited wholesale value times the same retail mark-up the effect uses, as the family recipe asks) and the members' and pantries' cost of handing it out. Credit goes by share of resources, so Feeding America is credited with about 4% of the food's value. The programs line's child hunger and food-as-medicine grants pay for handing out network food to children and patients (backpacks, school and clinic pantries), so they are part of this branch's cost and its food.

rows.label: SNAP: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The network's own count of applications helped, with no published audit; the benefit and its value are from national data. 0.8, range 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: SNAP: share of the enrolments that the help caused
rows.explainer: Anchored on the one trial of SNAP application help, Finkelstein and Notowidigdo 2019 (NBER w24652): enrolment among eligible older people was 6% in the control group and 18% with information plus application help, so two thirds of the assisted group's enrolments were caused by the help. People who come to a food bank for help are readier to apply on their own, so a smaller share: 0.35, range 0.15 to 0.65.

rows.label: SNAP: Feeding America's share of the resources behind the network's SNAP help
rows.explainer: Feeding America's share of the resources behind the network's SNAP help: its own cost on SNAP over the cost of all the help (Convention 2), so the credit follows the cost assumed to go to SNAP.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment: share of the food passed on that is eaten
rows.explainer: Share of the food passed on that reaches households: some donated food spoils or is thrown away at the food bank or pantry (much is near its date). 0.95, range 0.85 to 0.99. Food unused at home is in inkind_cash_equivalence, not here. Food only.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: Feeding America's money is not replaced by government; its grants may pull in members' own money (above 1) or fund what they would have paid for anyway (below). As the Salvation Army build.

rows.label: Years a dollar given waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Net assets over a year's cash spending: about a year and a half of money in hand, so a gift is spent that much later on average.

rows.label: Discount for the wait before a gift is spent
Food: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the pounds are audited, but who eats the food is spread over a national estimate of participants and its value to them (retail mark-up, in-kind discount) is a judgment, with no measurement for Feeding America's food.

rows.label: SNAP: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the applications are the network's count, approvals and the share caused are judged from one trial of other outreach.

rows.label: Food: adjustments combined
rows.formula: food_evidence_adj * food_counterfactual_adj * food_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * food_missing_data_adj

rows.label: SNAP: adjustments combined
rows.formula: snap_evidence_adj * snap_counterfactual_adj * snap_attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * snap_missing_data_adj

Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: (-) donated food that displaces grocers' sales and so some farm and store income, and pantry food replacing what families would have got from other charities, -1%; (+) volunteers' own wellbeing from volunteering, not counted, up to +3%. -1%, range -5% to +5%. Not here: the grants' help to members moving their own food (their cost is already in the resource-share credit), the child hunger and food-as-medicine grants (part of the food branch), and food kept out of landfill (its own row, below).

rows.label: Tonnes per pound

source.title: NIST, SI units: mass (the international avoirdupois pound)
source.page: the pound is defined as exactly 0.453 592 37 kilogram

rows.explainer: The definition of the pound, to turn the pounds of donated food into metric tonnes of food kept out of the waste stream.

rows.label: Share of the donated food that would otherwise have gone to landfill
rows.explainer: Without donation, unsold food from manufacturers and retailers goes partly to landfill and partly to animal feed, composting, anaerobic digestion or salvage sellers; in the US most wasted food is landfilled. 30%, range 10% to 60%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO2e from landfilling a tonne of food (net of landfill gas capture)
rows.explainer: Food in a landfill rots into methane, part of it captured. EPA's Waste Reduction Model puts landfilled food waste at roughly half a tonne of CO2e per short ton, net of gas capture; 0.5, range 0.3 to 0.8 (lower with good capture, higher over 20 years). The emissions of producing the food are not counted: the food was produced either way.

rows.label: Food: landfill emissions averted, Feeding America's credit (t CO2e)
rows.formula: fa_pounds * tonnes_per_pound * landfill_share * tco2e_per_tonne_food_landfilled * food_counterfactual_adj * food_attribution_share * food_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: A side effect: food passed on instead of landfilled, with Feeding America's credit share, the share that it caused and the missing-data step of the food branch.

Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tonnes' bridge, as by the tco2e unit's conversion: 0, since food rotting in a landfill burns no fuel and carries no smoke (its methane's ozone is counted through the methane share below).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: Deaths a source counts directly beside the tonnes; 0 when the smoke is in air_pollution_weight, so nothing is counted twice.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.explainer: The share of these tonnes (in CO₂e) that is methane, which the site's climate conversion values by methane's own timing: earlier, shorter warming and the ozone it makes (docs/normalization.md 2.5). Food rotting in a landfill gives off methane; its CO₂ is from plants and isn't counted, so the landfill tonnes are nearly all methane, less the fuel of hauling it and the power credited to captured landfill gas in EPA's Waste Reduction Model. Our judgment, 0.95 (0.85 to 1).

rows.label: Landfill emissions averted, in tonnes of CO2e (after adjustments)
Climate, in healthy years
rows.formula: tco2e_bridged * (($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier) / ($uov_per_daly)
rows.explainer: The bridge from t CO₂e into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.
